how_it_is_used: bie/brain/visual_thinking.py: the 'dikhane ki soch' step names, for every beat, its key idea, its relation (one of the ids below, or 'other' with a note, which is logged) and the things, people and places it names. The entry for the relation says how the relation is SHOWN; the things are shown as themselves (an icon or a picture found by code in the icon index and the asset library, never a word standing for the thing). Screen text is a name or a short natural phrase, never a sentence: the sentence lives in the narration and the subtitles (page-2 principle).

picture_types.timeline: a book timeline (dated markers) drawn with the timeline_build block: the book's years and labels, nothing added
picture_types.gallery: a book panel of items (the six Evolution-of-Money pictures, the five currencies) drawn as a numbered row of icon cards: the thing's icon and its name under it
picture_types.table: a book table drawn as itself, row by row on the words that say the rows
picture_types.flow: a book flow (boxes joined by arrows) drawn with the flow_build block
picture_types.tree: a classification or structure drawn as a tree
picture_types.chart: numbers over years drawn as a chart

rules.rule: Every beat shows at least one non-text thing tied to its nouns or its relation (an icon, a mark, an arrow, a crowd or value step, a table row, a picture event; in a world a prop, a person, a price or a crowd step), cued on a word of that beat. A beat that only adds text is refused.

The screen never shows text alone for more than 10 seconds: while a beat is spoken, the thing it names is on screen (Navin, 30 October 2026: 'sirf text hi text screen par dikha to video ... ek book ban jaayegi').

Screen text is a name or a short natural phrase (at most 8 words; a board 2 lines of 28 characters), never a sentence: the sentence lives in the narration and the subtitles. The picture shows the thing itself, so its label is understood without reading (page-2 principle).

A book diagram or table the part covers is drawn as itself: a timeline with the book's years and labels, a table row by row, a panel of items as a gallery of icon cards, a flow as boxes and arrows. Code places it; the plan builds around it and never leaves it out.

A world (C) is used only when the beats are the story of the concept's real-world example with actors at a place, and that place comes from the example itself, never from a keyword of the narration; the same world kit is never used in two consecutive parts.
A caution, caveat or fact-check line ('illustrative numbers', 'imagined market', 'data not given', 'outside clarification') never appears on screen: it stays a background check in the records.

A beat that tells a process (paying and getting change, a UPI scan, a card tap, a cheque, a barter swap, a refusal, counting up to a limit, counting) shows it HAPPENING with its kriya ka saancha: the people act on their cue words (hands give and take, the phone is raised to the QR stand, a head shakes), the camera moves in to the hands and the screen and back out (Navin, 1 November 2026: 'process show nahi ho rahi hai, like upi payment ka jikar hai shop par, par agar wo visuals se clear ho jaise scanner phone scan, tab maja hai'). A process no saancha fits goes to the missing-capability log.
rules.check: bie/brain/visual_thinking.py check_ideas (template per beat); bie/brain/video/saanche.py problems_of

rules.rule: Story goods come from the story: a shop's stock, the buyers' bags, a balance's pans and an action's objects are the things the beat names (salt for salt, cloth for cloth), from the icon index and the asset library; nothing is drawn from a fixed picture (Navin, 1 November 2026: 'baat ho rahi hai kapda khareedne ki namak khareedne ki aur wo wahi cheeni ko show kar rha hai'). A thing no source has goes to needs.json.

Layout in every mode: boards, labels, price tags, balances and actions never overlap while on screen together; in a world at most one board, label or title is on screen at a time and numbers go on objects (a price tag, the note, the phone screen, a passbook), never on a label; nothing sits under the subtitle strip (the bottom 14 % of the frame); an action's people are at least about a quarter of the frame tall; no camera key shows an empty street.
rules.check: bie/brain/video/world.py layout_problems; bie/brain/canvas.py subtitle_problems, above_strip, auto_camera

rules.rule: Meaning: every relation of the dikhane ki list is realised by an element on its beat (a refusal or 'no status' puts a cross on that thing; an acceptance a tick; a limit a meter stopping at its red line); a struck value with an up or down arrow only when the same quantity changes, and change given back is the pay_change saancha (Navin's D1 findings 4 and 5).

One main character per video: the person the story follows keeps the same face, clothes and cap in every part; the others are generic. Icons fit the era and the concept (a phone or a card in a barter beat is reported).

processes.how_it_is_used: bie/brain/video/saanche.py TEMPLATES: the visual-idea step picks one per beat (template; 'none', or 'other' with a note that goes to the missing-capability log); the maker draws it as an action node (canvas) or element (world); code times the steps and moves the camera in to it.

hand_over.shows: A gives a thing to B

pay_change.shows: the buyer pays a note, takes the goods and gets the change back (₹500 in, ₹200 back)

barter_swap.shows: two people swap their things; at 'ask' both wonder whether they want the other's thing

upi.shows: the buyer's phone scans the shop's QR stand; the phone shows '₹300 paid', the shopkeeper's 'received'

card_tap.shows: a card taps the shop's POS machine; the machine shows the amount approved

cheque.shows: a cheque is written for the amount, handed to the bank, and the two passbooks change (payer down, payee up)

coin_count.shows: coins drop onto a pile while a meter rises; at 'limit' it stops at its red line

refuse.shows: the person looks at the thing, shakes the head, and a cross lands on the thing

accept.shows: the person looks at the thing, nods, and a tick lands on the thing

count_stack.shows: n things appear one by one as they are said
